source_text: Τὸ γὰρ πόνῳ κτηθὲν, περιχαρῶς ὑπεδέχθη καὶ φιλοπόνως διεφυλάχθη· ὧν μέντοι πρόχειρος ὁ πορισμὸς, τούτων ἡ κτῆσις εὐκαταφρόνητος. Διὰ τοῦτο ὁδῷ τινι καὶ τάξει ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν περὶ τοῦ Μονογενοῦς ἔννοιαν προσβι βάζει. Καίτοιγε τοῦ ἐν φωνῇ λόγου οὐδὲ οὕτως ἦν χρεία τῇ ἀσωμάτῳ φύσει, αὐτῶν τῶν νοηθέντων μεταδίδοσθαι δυναμένων τῷ συνεργοῦντι. Ὥστε τίς χρεία λόγου τοῖς δυναμένοις ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ νοήματος κοινωνεῖν ἀλλήλοις τῶν βουλευμάτων; Φωνὴ μὲν γὰρ δι' ἀκοὴν, καὶ ἀκοὴ φωνῆς ἕνεκεν. Ὅπου δὲ οὐκ ἀὴρ, οὐχὶ γλῶσσα, οὐχὶ οὖς, οὐ πόρος σκολιὸς ἐπὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ συναίσθησιν ἀναφέρων τοὺς ψόφους, ἐκεῖ οὐδὲ ῥημάτων χρεία, ἀλλ' ἐξ αὐτῶν, ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις, τῶν ἐν καρδίᾳ νοημάτων τοῦ θελήματος ἡ μετά δοσις. Ὅπερ οὖν ἔφην, ὥστε διαναστῆναι τὸν νοῦν ἡμῶν πρὸς τὴν ἔρευναν τοῦ προσώπου πρὸς ὃν οἱ λόγοι, σοφῶς καὶ ἐντέχνως τὸ σχῆμα τοῦτο τῆς διαλέκτου παρείληπται. 3.3 Δεύτερόν ἐστιν ἐξετάσαι, εἰ ἕτερον παρὰ τὸν ἐν ἀρχῇ πεποιημένον οὐρανὸν τὸ στερέωμα τοῦτο, ὃ καὶ αὐτὸ ἐπεκλήθη οὐρανὸς, καὶ εἰ ὅλως οὐρανοὶ δύο· ὅπερ οἱ τὰ περὶ οὐρανοῦ φιλοσοφήσαντες ἕλοιντ' ἂν μᾶλλον τὰς γλώσσας προέσθαι, ἢ ὡς ἀληθὲς παραδέξασθαι. Ἕνα γὰρ ὑποτίθενται οὐρανὸν, καὶ οὐκ ἔχειν αὐτῷ φύσιν, δεύτερον, ἢ τρίτον, ἢ πολλοστὸν προσγενέσθαι, πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ οὐρανίου σώματος εἰς τὴν τοῦ ἑνὸς σύστασιν ἀπαναλωθείσης, ὡς οἴονται. Ἓν γάρ φασι τὸ κυκλοφορικὸν σῶμα, καὶ τοῦτο πεπερασμένον· ὅπερ εἰ συναπήρτισται τῷ πρώτῳ οὐρανῷ, μηδὲν ὑπολείπεσθαι πρὸς δευτέρου ἢ τρίτου γένεσιν. Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν οἱ ὕλην ἀγέννητον ἐπεισάγοντες τῷ δημιουργῷ φαντάζονται, ἐκ τῆς πρώτης μυθοποιίας πρὸς τὸ ἀκόλουθον ψεῦδος ὑποφερόμενοι· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀξιοῦμεν τοὺς τῶν Ἑλλήνων σοφοὺς, μὴ πρότερον ἡμᾶς καταχλευάζειν πρὶν τὰ πρὸς ἀλλήλους διάθωνται. Εἰσὶ γὰρ ἐν αὐτοῖς οἳ ἀπείρους οὐρανοὺς καὶ κόσμους εἶναί φασιν, ὧν ὅταν ἀπελέγξωσιν τὸ ἀπίθανον οἱ ἐμβριθεστέραις ταῖς ἀποδείξεσι χρώμενοι, καὶ ταῖς γεωμετρικαῖς ἀνάγκαις συστήσωσι μὴ ἔχειν φύσιν ἄλλον οὐρανὸν γενέσθαι παρὰ τὸν ἕνα, τότε καὶ μᾶλλον καταγελασόμεθα τῆς γραμμικῆς καὶ ἐντέχνου αὐτῶν φλυαρίας, εἴπερ ὁρῶντες πομφόλυγας διὰ τῆς ὁμοίας αἰτίας γινομένας μίαν τε καὶ πολλὰς, εἶτα ἀμφιβάλλουσι περὶ οὐρανῶν πλειόνων, εἰ ἐξαρκεῖ αὐτοὺς ἡ δημιουργικὴ δύναμις παραγαγεῖν εἰς τὸ εἶναι. Ὧν τὴν ἰσχὺν καὶ τὸ μέγεθος οὐδὲν ἡγούμεθα διαφέρειν τῆς κοίλης νοτίδος τῆς ὑπερφυσωμένης ἐν τοῖς κρουνοῖς, ὅταν πρὸς τὴν ὑπεροχὴν τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ δυνάμεως ἀποβλέψωμεν. Ὥστε καταγέλαστος αὐτοῖς ὁ τοῦ ἀδυνάτου λόγος. Ἡμεῖς δὲ τοσοῦτον ἀπέχομεν τῷ δευτέρῳ ἀπιστεῖν, ὅτι καὶ τὸν τρίτον ἐπιζητοῦμεν, οὗ τῆς θέας ὁ μακάριος Παῦλος ἠξιώθη. Ὁ δὲ ψαλμὸς ὀνομάζων οὐρανοὺς οὐρανῶν, καὶ πλειόνων ἡμῖν ἔννοιαν ἐνεποίησε. Οὐ δήπου δὲ ταῦτα παραδοξότερα τῶν ἑπτὰ κύκλων, καθ' ὧν οἱ ἑπτὰ ἀστέρες σχεδὸν παρὰ πάντων συμφώνως ὁμολογοῦνται φέρεσθαι, οὓς καὶ ἐνηρμόσθαι φασὶν ἑτέρῳ τὸν ἕτερον, κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα τῶν κάδων τῶν εἰς ἀλλήλους ἐμβεβηκότων. Τούτους δὲ τὴν ἐναντίαν τῷ παντὶ φερο μένους, περισχιζομένου τοῦ αἰθέρος αὐτοῖς, εὔηχόν τινα καὶ ἐναρμόνιον ἀποδιδόναι φθόγγον, ὥστε πᾶσαν τὴν ἐν μελῳδίαις ἡδονὴν ὑπερβάλλειν.
thought_title: The purpose of God's spoken word and the question of multiple heavens
orientation: Basil is explaining why Genesis presents God as speaking during creation, then turns to ask whether the firmament is a second heaven distinct from the one made in the beginning.
pass_a_gloss: For what is acquired with toil is received with great joy and guarded with diligence; but of those things whose acquisition is ready at hand, the possession is easily despised. For this reason he leads us by a certain path and order to the thought about the only Son. And yet there was not even so any need of spoken word for the incorporeal nature, since the very things thought are able to be shared with the co-worker. So what need is there of speech for those who are able to share their counsels with one another from the very thought itself? For voice is for the sake of hearing, and hearing for the sake of voice. But where there is no air, no tongue, no ear, no winding passage carrying sounds up to the perception in the head, there is no need of words either, but the sharing of the will comes from the very thoughts in the heart, as one might say. So then, as I said, in order to rouse our mind to the search for the person to whom the words are addressed, this form of discourse has been wisely and skillfully employed. Second, it is necessary to examine whether this firmament, which was itself also called heaven, is other than the heaven made in the beginning, and whether there are altogether two heavens; which thing those who have philosophized about heaven would rather give up their tongues than accept as true. For they posit one heaven, and that it has no nature for a second or third or many more to be added, since all the substance of the heavenly body was used up, as they think, in the constitution of the one. For they say the revolving body is one, and this is finite; which if it was fully completed in the first heaven, nothing is left over for the generation of a second or third. These things then those who introduce unbegotten matter to the creator imagine, being carried down from the first myth-making to the consequent falsehood; but we ask the wise men of the Greeks not to mock us before they settle things among themselves. For there are among them those who say that the heavens and worlds are infinite; when those who use weightier demonstrations refute their unpersuasiveness, and by geometrical necessities establish that it is not possible in nature for another heaven to come into being besides the one, then we shall laugh all the more at their linear and artful nonsense, if indeed seeing bubbles produced by the same cause, one and many, they then doubt about more heavens, whether the creative power is sufficient to bring them into being. Whose strength and size we consider to differ in nothing from the hollow moisture blown up in springs, when we look to the surpassing greatness of the power of God. So that their argument of impossibility is laughable. But we are so far from disbelieving the second, that we seek also the third, of which the blessed Paul was deemed worthy of the sight. And the psalm naming heavens of heavens has also produced in us the thought of more. These things are surely not more incredible than the seven circles, on which the seven stars are agreed by nearly all to be carried, which they say are fitted one into another, according to the image of jars fitted into one another. And these, being carried in the direction opposite to the whole, while the ether is split around them, give back a certain melodious and harmonious sound, so as to surpass all pleasure in melodies.

choices.why: Basil uses this term for the Son as the one to whom the Father speaks in creation; 'co-worker' preserves the active partnership implied by the participle.
Basil describes the physical ear canal; 'winding passage' keeps the anatomical concreteness and the adjective's force.
Basil refers to the narrative device of God speaking; 'form of discourse' captures the rhetorical register without implying mere ornament.
Basil attacks the Greek philosophical doctrine of eternal matter; 'unbegotten' is the standard patristic term and matches the glossary's concern with origins.
Basil mocks the geometric proofs of the philosophers; 'linear' preserves the technical-geometrical flavor of the Greek.
This is the literal LXX phrase Basil quotes; keeping the doubled genitive preserves the scriptural idiom.

pass_b_english: What is gained by labor is received with great joy and guarded with diligence, while what comes easily is held cheaply. For this reason Scripture leads us forward by a kind of path and order toward the knowledge of the only Son. And yet the incorporeal nature had no need of spoken words even so, since the very things conceived could be communicated directly to the co-worker. What need would there be for speech among those who can share their counsels with one another from the thought itself? For voice exists for hearing, and hearing for voice. But where there is no air, no tongue, no ear, no winding passage carrying sounds up to the perception in the head, there is no need of words either; the intention is communicated, one might say, from the very thoughts in the heart. So, as I said, this form of discourse has been wisely and skillfully employed in order to rouse our minds to search for the person to whom the words are addressed.

The second question to examine is whether this firmament, which was itself also called heaven, is different from the heaven made in the beginning, and whether there are in fact two heavens. The philosophers of heaven would sooner surrender their tongues than accept this as true. They posit one heaven, and say it has no nature capable of admitting a second, or third, or many more, since all the substance of the heavenly body was used up, as they think, in the constitution of the one. For they say there is one revolving body, and it is finite; and if this was completely fitted together with the first heaven, nothing is left over for the generation of a second or third. These are the imaginings of those who introduce unbegotten matter to the Creator, carried from their first myth-making into the falsehood that follows from it. But we ask the wise men of the Greeks not to mock us before they settle their disputes with one another. For among them there are some who say the heavens and worlds are infinite; and when those who use weightier proofs refute their implausibility and establish by geometric necessities that no other heaven can by nature come into being besides the one, then we will laugh all the more at their geometric and artful nonsense—if, seeing bubbles produced by the same cause, one and many alike, they still doubt about multiple heavens, whether the creative power suffices to bring them into being. When we look to the surpassing power of God, we consider the strength and magnitude of these heavens to differ in no way from the hollow moisture blown up in fountains. So their argument from impossibility is laughable. We, however, are so far from disbelieving in the second that we seek also the third, the vision of which the blessed Paul was counted worthy to receive. And the psalm, naming the heavens of heavens (Psalm 148:4), has given us the idea of still more. Surely these things are no more extraordinary than the seven circles, on which nearly all agree the seven stars are carried, and which they say are fitted one into another, like the image of jars set inside one another. These, moving in a direction opposite to the whole, while the ether is parted by them, produce a clear and harmonious sound, surpassing every pleasure found in melodies.

problems.why: 'θελήματος' means 'will' but context is about communication of thoughts/counsels between Father and Son; 'will' suggests volition rather than shared intention/plan.
problems.fix: the intention is communicated, one might say, from the very thoughts in the heart

problems.quote: they still doubt whether the creative power is sufficient to bring multiple heavens into being
problems.source_quote: εἶτα ἀμφιβάλλουσι περὶ οὐρανῶν πλειόνων, εἰ ἐξαρκεῖ αὐτοὺς ἡ δημιουργικὴ δύναμις παραγαγεῖν εἰς τὸ εἶναι
problems.why: αὐτοὺς refers to the heavens, not the philosophers; the question is whether creative power suffices to bring the heavens into being.
problems.fix: they still doubt about multiple heavens, whether the creative power suffices to bring them into being
problems.ruling: αὐτοὺς is accusative, must refer to οὐρανῶν (heavens), not philosophers; English misassigns referent.

problems.quote: was entirely used up in the first heaven
problems.why: 'συναπήρτισται' means 'was fitted together with/attached to,' not 'used up in.' The argument is that if the finite revolving body was completely fitted to/constituted as the first heaven, nothing remains.
problems.fix: if this was completely fitted together with the first heaven
problems.ruling: συναπήρτισται means 'fitted together with/attached to,' not 'used up'; ἀπαναλωθείσης (used up) appears earlier but not here.

edits.old: they still doubt whether the creative power is sufficient to bring multiple heavens into being
edits.new: they still doubt about multiple heavens, whether the creative power suffices to bring them into being

edits.old: if this was entirely used up in the first heaven

fixed: Changed 'the will is transmitted' to 'the intention is communicated' because the source 'τοῦ θελήματος ἡ μετάδοσις' refers to the sharing of a plan or intention between Father and Son, not mere volition.

Changed 'they still doubt whether the creative power is sufficient to bring multiple heavens into being' to 'they still doubt about multiple heavens, whether the creative power suffices to bring them into being' because the pronoun 'αὐτοὺς' refers to the heavens, not the philosophers.

Changed 'if this was entirely used up in the first heaven' to 'if this was completely fitted together with the first heaven' because 'συναπήρτισται' means 'was fitted together with' or 'attached to,' not 'used up in.'

problems.why: ἐντέχνος means 'skillful, artful' but here ironically; 'artful nonsense' captures this. However, 'linear' for γραμμικῆς is odd—γραμμικός relates to lines/geometry, i.e., 'geometric' or 'diagram-based'. 'Linear' in modern English suggests one-dimensional or sequential, which misleads. The Greek refers to their geometric/line-drawing proofs.
problems.ruling: γραμμικῆς means 'geometric/line-based'; 'linear' misleads modern readers as sequential, not geometric proofs.

fixed: Changed 'linear' to 'geometric' because γραμμικῆς refers to their geometric/line-drawing proofs, not one-dimensional or sequential reasoning.

refereed.quote: the heavens and worlds are infinite
refereed.source_quote: ἀπείρους οὐρανοὺς καὶ κόσμους εἶναί φασιν
refereed.why: Source says 'infinite heavens and worlds'; English reverses the adjective's target.
refereed.fix: the heavens and worlds are infinite
refereed.ruling: ἀπείρους modifies both οὐρανοὺς and κόσμους; English 'heavens and worlds are infinite' misplaces it.
